participants: Chris Klevan (sales manager, running the meeting)
summary: Daily sales team meeting: wins round, an intro for a second new setter (Adam A., 27, two years in sales, DM setter), projection updates, a short operational discussion about getting prospect phone numbers into the booking system, and then an extended one-to-one roleplay between Chris Klevan and Richard Claessen on selling to high performers. Andrew Musial is at $20k cash and four units and needs two more; Richard is at one unit and $1,200 cash collected and commits to opening his calendar from 12pm and working the weekend. Derek Harris is set a KPI of three sets per day, six sets this week and 15 per week after, at an assumed 20% set-to-close rate. The roleplay has Chris playing a 37-year-old Michelin-starred restaurant owner who is already optimised, and the coaching that follows is the most substantive script material in the batch: do not run a consequence frame on a prideful high performer, do not ask 'why now' of someone whose identity is taking action, and reframe problem questions as 'what's not quite at the level you'd like it to be'. Two conduct disclosures surfaced in passing — a setter confirming he speaks as Trevor in voice messages, and a permissive exchange about stimulant use to improve closing.
notable: SETTER IDENTITY: Adam A. confirmed he sends prospect voice messages in Trevor's persona. Richard: "And you're Trevor, right? Like, you're Trevor. Just to check." Adam: "I'm Trevor? What do you mean?" Richard: "Yeah. As in, like, you talk as Trevor in the VMs." Adam: "Oh, yeah. I talk as Trevor." Richard: "Okay. It's good to know. Perfect." Chris Klevan, present throughout: "Sweet. Awesome. Good stuff." Nobody treated it as an issue.

PAYMENT PLANS EXIST IN PRACTICE: Richard referenced both a deposit and a six-instalment plan for a live deal — "I thought I was going to lose a deposit, there's a big chance I can still get him in on Friday, because he cannot pay [in] six times" and "I've got the deposit that's like 99% coming in." Two days earlier he told a prospect on a live call: "We don't have anything, like, set in stone."

Richard described the previous day's firefighter close (Jake Brenner) in terms of how easy the safety risk made it: "I had this call yesterday with a firefighter. Like, he was like, yeah, I'm just, I'm really not showing up well. I'm not helping the people. Like, I'm putting other people at risk. It's so easy to then close them... As in, like, he isn't fit. So he is putting other people's lives in danger."

Andrew Musial relayed a story about a closer performing best on "a little line of cocaine and a beer"; Chris Klevan responded that the team is free to do what it feels is necessary provided KPIs are met, and separately disclosed he has psilocybin mushrooms he has not taken.

SETTER KPIs recorded: three sets per day per setter; projections built at roughly 20% set-to-close; Derek Harris scheduled for six sets this week, then 15 per week, three units, ten units for the month.

Setters have edit access to all closers' calendars and mark sets with their own initials — this is the mechanical origin of the KFS/KL/DH title suffixes: "you edit it, you put your initials on there, you hit don't send". Derek was given access to Michael's, Richard's and Andrew's calendars.

Prospect phone numbers entered at booking are not propagating into the system, so closers cannot pre-confirm DM-set calls. Richard: "It does say the attendee, but it doesn't say their phone number... I also don't see any phone number here." Richard pre-contacts prospects to raise show rates: "just so that they at least know who I am will always help increasing the show rate anyway."

Chris Klevan's high-performer coaching adds material not present in playbook.json: do not run the Phase 5 consequence frame on a prideful high performer ("consequence doesn't really work on people in Pride"), do not ask 'why now' of someone whose self-concept is always taking action ("it actually challenges their ego"), and replace 'what's not going well' with 'what's not quite at the level you'd like it to be'.

Chris's stated selling philosophy again: "seek to understand the truth, and show them the truth. Stay 100% committed to the truth", and on high performers "they'll typically just piff it and be done with it. They won't have to talk to a wife."
Richard notes a geographic close-rate difference: "maybe I get more Europeans, they're a little bit harder to close because they don't have financing."
Richard names high performers as the prospect type he is most afraid of and Chris assigns him homework to deliberately take those calls and bring the sticking points back.
